newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to seek global treaty on banning land mines.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to seek global treaty on banning land mines.

text.p: President Bill Clinton has decided the United States will seek negotiations on a global treaty to ban anti-personnel land mines, the White House said on Friday.

"The president today is announcing that when the conference on disarmament opens its 1997 session in Geneva on Monday the United States will seek to initiate negotiations on a worldwide treaty banning the use, production, stockpiling and transfer of anti-personnel land mines," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said in his daily briefing.

"We've got some ideas on how in pursuing this goal we can do some things on our own unilaterally that will create a better environment in order to achieve that type of ban," McCurry said. "The United States will observe a permanent ban on the export and transfer of anti-personnel land mines."

"We would also at the same time urge other nations to join us in stopping the export and transfer of these mines," he added. "We believe that will help hasten the completion of a comprehensive ban and in the process save many ... lives."
McCurry also said that the United States has decided to cap its own anti-personnel landmine stockpile at its current level, which officials put at several million.

National Security Council official Bob Bell said the administration had concluded the conference on disarmament was the best forum in which to pursue the negotiations, although he said the United States would support Canada's so-called "Ottowa process" of talks seeking a similar end.
